concord

/KON-kord/ - the stress falls on KON · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Concord means a formal state of peace and agreement between parties — harmony with the weight of a treaty behind it.

After the fence settlement, the two farms entered a long concord — gates left unlocked, machinery lent both ways.

Example

For a century the two villages had fought over the high pasture; the concord that followed the 1911 agreement held so well that their children now share a single schoolhouse on the pasture road.

Concord names the state, not the paper: parties once at odds, now genuinely at ease with each other. Its unit-mate accord is the document you sign; concord is the weather that follows — harmony you can live inside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

harmony: Harmony is the everyday word for parts agreeing sweetly — voices in a choir, colors in a room, flavors in a dish — and it needs no history behind it. Concord is grander and more formal: a settled peace between parties who once quarreled, with the ease of people who have genuinely put a fight behind them.

amity: Amity is friendly relations, especially between nations — the diplomatic warmth of allies who simply get along. Concord runs deeper and carries a memory: the parties were once at odds, and the quarrel has healed. Amity never needed a fight; concord is peace after one.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

strife: open struggling against each other

friction: the constant small rubbing of parties not at ease

Where it sits · how fully the sides come together

truce → concord → unity

truce vs. concord: A truce stops far short of concord — it only stops the shooting, with the quarrel paused rather than healed, while concord means the parties have grown genuinely easy with each other.

unity vs. concord: Unity goes further than concord — in concord the parties remain themselves, at peace; in unity the border between them is gone altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-: together

Root — cord-: heart

Put it together: Con- (together) + cord- (heart) = hearts together. Latin concordia was the Romans' own name for civic peace — they built her a temple after their worst quarrels. The word still means exactly that: separate hearts keeping one rhythm. Flip the prefix to dis- and the hearts pull apart — discord.

Use the root in a new word: discord: One sour trumpet filled the hall with discord until the conductor stopped the piece.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Concord is the lived state of harmony between parties — use it for the years of ease, not the signing day. The signing day belongs to accord. Harmony is the everyday word and covers music and color; amity is warm diplomacy between states. Concord carries the memory of a quarrel outgrown.
